utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the registrar call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. This is case number IT-00-39 & 40-PT, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik and Biljana Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The appearances.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Judge May. My name is Mark Harmon, appearing for the Prosecutor. Appearing with me, to my right, is Mr. Thomas Hannis, and to my left, Ms. Carmela Annink-Javier.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Deyan Brashich, along with Nikola Kostich, for the Krajisnik defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Eugene O'Sullivan and Peter Murphy appearing for Biljana Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is a case which is listed for a Status Conference today, the purpose being to get this matter ready for trial, to fix a date for a Pre-Trial Conference, and generally to hear what the state of preparedness is of the various parties. A date for trial, it had been hoped, could be fixed in November. That looks as though it may not be a possibility, in which case I have in mind a Pre-Trial Conference in November with a view to a trial starting in January. That would be the current programme. I understand there are difficulties in preparation of this case, it's not yet ready, so two more months will be available for preparation time. It may be best if we start with the Prosecution, and I'll hear from Mr. Harmon on the state of preparation there. I should say that I've read the transcript of the 65 ter conference with the Senior Legal Officer yesterday so I have some idea of the various issues that were raised there and some of which can be resolved today.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Judge May, there are three principal issues, I think, that need to be addressed at this point that impinge on the readiness of the case to proceed to trial. The first is the issue of adjudicated facts. The Prosecutor's Office, as Your Honour knows, through the history of these proceedings, has endeavoured to reduce the size of this trial and the length of this trial by utilising tools that are embedded in the Rules to reduce the size of this trial. Under Rule 94, adjudicated facts, we submitted, over two years ago, the first set of adjudicated facts to the Defence. That was on the 21st of September, 2000, when we submitted 537 proposed adjudicated facts. We followed that up on the 14th of December, 2000, by filing an additional 33 proposed adjudicated facts. And on the 10th of December, 2001, we submitted to the Defence 408 additional facts. And our final submission of adjudicated facts to the Defence was on the 28th of March, 2002, when we submitted 384 proposed adjudicated facts. The Plavsic Defence has responded, a long time ago, giving us their position on each of those facts. The Krajisnik Defence has responded to 380 of the proposed 1.363 adjudicated facts, and as Your Honour knows, this has been a subject of discussion on numerous occasions. In reviewing my notes, on the 10th of May Status Conference, you ordered the Defence to reply to the -- all of the adjudicated facts by the 30th of May. On 31 July, the recent 65 ter conference, it was agreed that the adjudicated facts on behalf of the Krajisnik Defence would most likely be concluded by the end of August. Now, the consequence of not having a response by the Krajisnik Defence is that we have deferred filing a motion in respect of those adjudicated facts under Rule 94(B) because we anticipated that we would have closure on an agreement on those facts. My point is that we have not been able to conclude that aspect of the Pre-Trial effort to reduce the size of this case, and we are now confronted with either an agreement that those -- that the Defence will -- in the Krajisnik case, will conclude its analysis of the remaining proposed adjudicated facts or we will file a motion to have the Court make a determination under Rule 94(B). So that's the status of the efforts that have been ongoing for over two years on the adjudicated facts. The second Rule that we have tried to use, and we have used with vigour, is Rule 92 bis, and in that respect, our witness list, which was submitted to the Trial Chamber with part of our pre-trial brief, identified approximately 406 witnesses, and we have identified 212 of those witnesses as 92 bis witnesses; in other words, 52 per cent of our witnesses. We have reached agreement with the Plavsic Defence on a significant number of those witnesses for 92 bis. They have agreed to accept the written evidence. There are some outstanding issues that need to be resolved with the Plavsic Defence in respect of those witnesses, and we have not reached agreement on any of the witnesses in respect of the Krajisnik Defence. The third issue that relates to pre-trial preparation has been expert reports, and we, Your Honour is well aware, have filed our expert reports well in advance of the time that normally is required for filing of expert reports. I think we have filed our first expert reports relating to exhumations in 2001; I don't have the exact dates, but a long, long time ago. And the court is aware of the history of this analysis by the Defence of these reports; some were filed in English, others were filed in B/C/S. The net result of the filings in respect of the reports in B/C/S was that an expert, a joint Defence expert, was appointed to analyse the reports in B/C/S, in an effort to find a resolution and hopefully an agreement that these would not be contested at trial. Unfortunately, the conclusion of the expert that led the Defence to -- led the Defence to agree that none of these reports would be accepted, that every autopsy report in those expert reports would be the subject of an examination and a cross-examination. Well, not wishing to leave the matter at that state of affairs, the Defence and I engaged in further discussions. Those discussions revealed a fundamental concern of the Defence, and that was were the incidents that were described in the indictment linked to the exhumation reports that -- of the experts that had been filed by us under Rule 94? With that issue now being addressed to the Prosecutor, I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. endeavoured to and then filed with the Defence, on the 9th of September of this year, a chart, a concise chart, listing the exhumations and the links between the exhumations and the events that are described in the indictment. That has been submitted to the Defence. That has been submitted to Ms. Featherstone. I'll give you an example of what I mean and what is included in this chart, Mr. President. The first incident that is revealed in the linkage chart relates to exhumation reports of Professor Wright and Dr. Hunt in respect of the Brcko exhumations. Both of those testimonies have been accepted previously in the Jelisic trial. The links and the events that are described in those particular exhumation reports relate to events that are contained in the Plavsic/Krajisnik indictment, and the links linking the event to the bodies that were found in the ground and that were exhumed is described in this chart. And the link, one of the principal links, between the events that were described in -- and I'll relate the scheduled incidents in the indictment: A.5.3, A.5.4 and B.4.1. Those are three separate events that took place in Brcko. The bodies that were exhumed in the mass grave were -- I'm sorry. The victims from those events were linked to the mass grave as a result of a schedule of bodies that were given to us by the Serbian authorities, saying -- it's a list saying these are the bodies that were found -- these are the bodies that were put in these graves. So these are the Serbian authorities themselves giving us the list of the victims who were put in this grave in the ground. Those bodies and those names relate back to the three incidents. So we have very clear linkage to the events in the indictment and the exhumations that were conducted by the experts. And you'll see, if Your Honour hasn't seen a copy of this, that each of those expert reports is described in it, and the event and the killing that is listed in the indictment is listed by incident, and on the right-hand column are the links, including the names of the witnesses and the physical evidence that link the grave to the event. So at this point in time, I know the Defence has just received this on September the 9th, and I am hopeful that there will be a resolution on this, but I do think, Mr. President, given the history of this, that it would be important to try to set a date by which we could have a decision by the Defence on whether or not they are prepared to accept these exhumation expert reports. Those are the three principal areas, Judge May, that have involved us over the past year and a half or two years in these proceedings, and in an attempt to get the length of the trial reduced, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Because if these aren't going to be accepted, they will have to be proven in the normal way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We're prepared to do that, Judge May. This is just a tool to make it easier. It seems to me -- it's our position, the Prosecutor's position, that this should not be a matter of contest, but that's not -- it's up to the Defence to make those decisions, not to me. We're prepared to prove everything in these exhumations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be that it's a straightforward matter which should be capable of agreement, one would imagine. But if it's not agreed, as often happens, then I'm afraid it must be proved in the usual way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We're prepared to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: As for the adjudicated facts, I'll hear what Mr. Brashich says. The position is that there has been a response on a third or so, roughly, but it may be that the remainder will have to be dealt with by way of ruling. There do seem to be a substantial number. I don't know if it's possible to cut that down for the Trial Chamber to look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We may do that in the course of filing our motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think it may be the simplest course, for you to file a motion, realistically. This matter has been going on long enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me deal with the 92 bis point, the statements under that Rule. You say you've reached agreement as to none with the Krajisnik Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: They have filed their objection to the -- all of the 92 bis statements that we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: All of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All of them. That's my recollection, and it's based on the fact that the statements deal with the acts or conduct of the accused and therefore are not subject to 92 bis. But I will defer to Mr. Brashich, who has taken the position and can articulate it more so. In the respect of the Plavsic defence, we've reached an agreement on many of these statements, and have over the past six months or one year that we've been involved in exchanging correspondence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Again, that may simply have to be a matter which is ruled on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Brashich, matters susceptible to agreement, the Court would encourage you to agree, if you can, what it is possible to agree. Of course you have the right to contest matters. The Defence always do. But a trial of this scope, one would think there must be some matters which can be agreed in order to shorten it and get to the real issues, which may be totally different.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm mindful of that fact. But to take the points raised by Mr. Harmon on an inverse basis: The Defence agreed to use a joint expert witness. We further agreed that that expert witness would deal with the documents in B/C/S. After the review by the expert, I consulted with him for a number of hours as to what he found at fault with the expert witness report. Based on Dr. Dunjic's advice to me, we took the position -- and if I do not heed the advice of our own expert in the particular field, I would not be serving Mr. Krajisnik very well. It was based on Dr. Dunjic's advice that the Prosecution's expert witness reports are wanting. I then told the Prosecution briefly what Dr. Dunjic had counselled the Krajisnik Defence, and that is a result of the chart which came into being on September 9th and got into our hands on the 12th or 13th of September. We have not been able to consult with Dr. Dunjic in the meantime. I will follow Dr. Dunjic's advice and do whatever is proper within the scope of the advice given. With regard to the 92 bis statements, I disagree with the position Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. taken by the Plavsic Defence. I find a number of the statements going directly to the guilt or the acts of my client, and the 92 bis statements, as constituted at this present time, are specifically referenced to counts in the indictment. Now, if the 92 bis statements are totally without the scope of the indictment, perhaps I would agree to let them in, but when they have been noted as supporting the allegations against my client in specific paragraphs of the indictment, then I will not agree to their introduction into evidence. With regard to the adjudicated facts, Your Honour has read the 65 ter conference transcript. The Defence is overwhelmed with the amount of material that we have had to face. We are short of resources, and we physically, and because of resources, could not and did not get to agreeing or disagreeing with the adjudicated facts. Now, that particular issue, the adjudicated facts, I had asked Mr. Kostich to address, and, again, as you ever read the transcript, he is at this present time without hours to address that particular issue. As the Court well noted, should we not be able to get to that task prior to a Pre-Trial Conference or well in advance of that Pre-Trial Conference, then the Court would have to rule on those 1.300 some odd adjudicated facts. One of the issues, Your Honour, is, of course, that this is not only a matter for counsel to pass upon, but each and every adjudicated fact would have to be discussed with the client. The other problem that we are faced with, Your Honour, is that these adjudicated facts are pregnant with innuendos and rather subjective interpretations of rulings made by this Trial Chamber or other Trial Chambers. So to parse the subjectivity and the intrusion of the Prosecution's point of view is a lengthy and time-consuming task, especially in light of the other tasks that the Defence is being charged with, including preparation of our case. Now, as Your Honour well knows, people forget, people get lost, and people die. That is the case with General Talic. So we have undertaken, well in advance, knowing that in a year and a half or whenever the Defence is called upon to put up its own evidence, that we have to be ready and that we do not lose it in the meantime. So our task has not only been preparation to meet the Prosecution's evidence but to look far ahead to our own affirmative defences. With regard to the adjudicated facts, I will again defer to Mr. Kostich, and I know that only one attorney per side but he has assured me -- I'll withdraw that. I will speak on behalf of Mr. Kostich. He has indicated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I will hear Mr. Kostich if you prefer he speaks on the matter because, clearly, if it can be resolved, as much as can be resolved as possible by agreement, the better for everybody. Mr. Kostich, ignoring - and I'm sure you will strike out those parts which you claim are innuendo or incorrect assertions - but concentrating on those matters which may be susceptible of agreement, do you think it's going to be possible to come to some further agreement or is it the position that you can get no further? It would certainly be helpful if you could make a good-faith attempt to get further on this issue. It would assist the trial, from everybody's point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTICH
utterances.text: You've indicated you've read my comments and Mr. Brashich's comments from the 65 ter. That has not changed. However, I appreciate the Court's concern in this area. What I will do is, regardless of what will happen in regard to the matter dealing with resources, the motion that's pending and so on, I will endeavour nevertheless to put this particular project at the top of the list, and I personally think that within approximately - today is the 20th - I would say that within the next 30 days, we can get a response to Mr. Harmon, OTP, just by doing it, and perhaps doing it in that fashion, I will endeavour to do that. It is of great concern. So I will do that, Judge, regardless of what occurs with regard to the other aspects of this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, thank you. Now, Mr. Brashich, the exhumation reports, I haven't followed the position here. You have your expert. He has asked for the originals of the report. Do I understand it right?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. The issue is, according to Dr. Dunjic, is the exhumation reports are not autopsy reports. There is no date of death, time of death, noted. This is one of his concerns, as I recall. Again, this was quite sometime ago, and I would have to refer to my notes of the meeting with Dr. Dunjic in Belgrade, but he had a list, a punch list, of problems that he had with the exhumation reports as such. I generally told Mr. Harmon as to those concerns, and that is when the linkage chart was produced. But it had nothing to do with the -- whether they were original or not reports. If I recall, according to my notes, there was also some issue as to colour photographs, but I believe that that was resolved. I just don't have my notes in front of me, Your Honour, on that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Harmon, it looks as though we are not going to get very much further. The sensible course may be for the matter to be prepared for trial, and it may be that during the course of the trial, some further resolution could take place. It really is a matter which should not be subject of lengthy evidence before the Trial Chamber, one would hope. It may be that the concerns which Mr. Brashich has ventilated can be brought to the attention of the Trial Chamber in due course and the evidence could be tailored in such a way that Dr. Dunjic can give the views, the witness could be - a witness, one would hope - could be cross-examined on these particular aspects of the case. [Microphone not activated] If there is no agreement, there is no agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In order to try to resolve this case as well, Judge May, I have invited the Defence to give me specific objections that relate to these exhumations so I can go back to the experts and say, "This is an objection. What say you?" And we could be involved in that kind of a dialogue. Unfortunately, I have never received any specific objections and therefore I am immobilised in terms of proceeding further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us proceed on that avenue. It seems the sensible one. And I'll raise it with Mr. Brashich. Mr. Brashich, I was going to raise it myself, but Mr. Harmon already has. Is there any reason why you can't send to the Prosecution the concerns which your expert has about these reports? It may be that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. they could be answered. It may be they can't be. But at least it would be possible to open a dialogue to see if there may be a simple answer, if one thinks of a difficulty, rather than having a witness brought here to give evidence to answer, "We don't know," or, "If there is an answer, I could just go and get the document," it would seem the sensible course is for you to put the concerns in a practical way to the Prosecution to resolve this. This is a matter of expert evidence, and it's outside the normal run of evidence, and it really should be, since it's between experts, susceptible to being dealt with before the trial and in a way which doesn't cause a lot of experts to have to come to give evidence unnecessarily. What I would have in mind would be to order something in the form of a list of interrogatories, or if you have questions or issues have been raised, for you to serve that on the Prosecution within the next ten days or so. For instance, it may be possible to extract part of what Dr. Dunjic has written to you to send to them. Now, I trust that that is a matter that can be pursued.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: I want to make it very clear, Your Honour, that I do not have a written report from Dr. Dunjic. I did not ask for a written report from him, and my communications with him with regard to his review of the Prosecution's expert witness reports was oral, and I only took some partial notes during that meeting. Therefore, what I am going to request of the expert witness, Dr. Dunjic, is to give me a wish list of the problems that he finds with the expert witness reports as now constituted. I cannot speak to him -- I cannot speak for him, whether that can be done within ten days. I myself cannot respond properly, since I am not qualified to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Well, Mr. Brashich, how long do you think it would take to get this report from him?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: I will try and contact Dr. Dunjic by telephone this afternoon and send a memo to chambers, if he can do it within 10, 15, 20 days, whatever the doctor advises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What I would order is that it be done within 21 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know that you can order that it be done within 21 days. I have no control over Dr. Dunjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure Dr. Dunjic would wish to cooperate. This is a trial which has gone on for a very long time. I have no doubt he's a busy expert, but nonetheless, I'm sure that he would wish to cooperate, and three weeks should be sufficient. He has told you what his concerns are. It's simply a matter of listing them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll pass the order on, in writing, to Dr. Dunjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. Now, that, I hope, will enable some progress to be made on that. We have -- the matter of the adjudicated facts you've heard about, the Defence response. The matter of the Rule 92 bis statements I think is out -- it will be a matter for the Trial Chamber. We have to resolve that. Now, I noticed there were two other matters at the conference yesterday which were raised. One was a matter to objections to individual pieces of evidence; for instance, the qualifications of experts and the admissibility of intercepts. Those matters, I'll hear what anybody wants to say about it, if they want to raise it, but it seems to me they are much more appropriately dealt with within the context of the trial itself, that the Trial Chamber which is dealing with the matter will have a far better grasp of the case inevitably, having heard some of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Your Honour, the concern that the Krajisnik Defence has is that in one of the particular submissions that we have made, I footnoted our reservation that in points of evidence, it might be better for the actual Trial Chamber to rule upon these issues. However, saying that, there are certain issues which I think should be resolved before trial, such as the intercept communications. That has the Chamber -- the Chamber has to pass upon foreign law that should be briefed. That should not occur during trial, because it will come to a dead stop. The same thing with regard to our motion, which is now in abeyance, with regard to the five-hour documentary, "The Death of Yugoslavia." Mr. Kostich and I have viewed that particular documentary. There is a host of translation problems. We are attempting to resolve that well in advance of trial, because if we don't resolve that in advance of trial, we are going to play the tape, and every three or four minutes Mr. Kostich and I will object, it will have to be rewound because what Mr. Milosevic said was not translated in the voiceover or it was mistranslated, and I can see wasting five to ten trial days just on an issue such as that. So I think that the Trial Chamber is correct in its position that a lot of rulings on evidence should take place during trial. However, mindful of the problems that we are faced with in a trial of this magnitude, certain things which could derail the trial should be properly addressed prior to trial, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I'll alert the Trial Chamber, obviously. That is a matter for it, and we will consider it and give our ruling on those matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, as far as this hearing is concerned, the one matter I want to raise is the question of a timetable, but it may be we can leave that until later. I have in mind a Pre-Trial Conference on the 14th of November. That is the date which has been identified. But there may be other matters which counsel want to raise before I rule on that. I'll start with the Prosecutor. Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The proposed date of the 14th of November, Your Honour, I'm weighing in relation to the adjudicated facts and the resolution of the adjudicated facts, which is, by Mr. Kostich's statement, 30 days from now he would attempt to bring closure to that subject. That would bring us to about the 20th of October. That leaves us little time to analyse - between the Pre-Trial Conference - to analyse the submission of Mr. Kostich and prepare a motion that would have to be ruled on, I think, by the Trial Chamber, as presently constituted, and I think that would impact on the trial and the possible length of the trial. I think Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the adjudicated facts is an important issue that needs to be resolved finally before we can have a meaningful Pre-Trial Conference. And so, as I say, working back to the date of 20 October, when Mr. Kostich says he could complete his work, leaves us precious little time to prepare the motion, have a hearing on the motion, get a decision on the motion, and then, based on whether the trial has been significantly shortened, have meaningful information from which to project a proper trial date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, it may be that that is an issue which can't be resolved, but we must do everything we can to get this matter on to trial. Putting things off is not going to assist. It may be that there will be issues still to be resolved even at the Pre-Trial Conference, in which case we'll have to deal with it as best we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We will wait for Mr. Kostich's answer and be guided accordingly. We may be filing a motion after the 20th of October, depending on the results of that discussion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: As far as the Defence are concerned, are there matters which they wish to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: No. There's only one matter, Your Honour, and that is the pre-trial brief which is due on the 30th. As you know from the transcript of the 65 ter conference, my computer system crashed on August 14th, Mr. Kostich's computer system crashed somewhat thereafter, and two disks which were specifically dedicated to the pre-trial brief failed. I was somewhat paranoid as all of these coincidences having occurred, but then there was a very large article in the New York Times Sunday Magazine which explained coincidences, so I've lost my paranoia. But we might be seeking a 10- or 15-day extension of time within which to file the Krajisnik Defence brief, Mr. Kostich and I working most of this afternoon and all day tomorrow on that issue. Seventy per cent of the material which was lost, not the pre-trial brief but general material in the Krajisnik case, has been retrieved from the hard drive. So I think, if we're lucky, we'll hit September 30th deadline. If we're not lucky, Your Honour, we're going to have to seek leave for a 10- to 15-day extension.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes. We have nothing specific to add at this time. Subject to what Mr. Brashich just said, it's our position that any briefs from the party should be filed on the same date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll fix the Pre-Trial Conference for the 14th of November, at 2.30, I think is the time we have the courtroom available. Mr. Brashich, are there any matters you wish to raise in relation to the conditions of detention of the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. The case is adjourned.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the Status Conference adjourned at
